doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

chapter: Big bands in the Bay Area
title: Bands visiting for movies: Glenn Miller, Barnet and the Palomar fire
summary: Before the war big bands came West mainly to make films; he saw Miller and Barnet and recalls the Palomar fire before Basie opened.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: But that’s what would happen here. See before the war, we didn’t have that many big bands. You had Vaudeville, but the only time you’d really have a big band would be when they came out to make a movie, see cause the transportation costs were prohibitive I guess at that time. So when there would be a picture, then the band, they would come right up the coast, up to Seattle and then back East again. The Glenn Miller band, they came here, I saw them over at Sweet’s Ballroom. They did a couple of pictures here. One was something about Sun Valley.
Sun Valley Serenade or something like that.

Yes, something like that. And Charlie Barnet’s band, I got to see them. As a matter of fact, Charlie Barnet, he was out here in 1939. So I guess he did a picture then. Because he played the old Palomar, before the Palladium in Los Angeles. And so the Palomar had Charlie Barnet, and see they used to broadcast and I would listen to them on the radio. Artie Shaw’s band was there, Buddy Rich was with him — I would listen to them, then Barnet’s band. Now Barnet, his closing night, he closed and Count Basie was supposed to open the following week. It would have been the first time a colored band had ever played the Palomar. But Basie was hot you know. So what happened? The place caught fire. And all of Barnet’s instruments were burned and the library. And what happened, they came up to Sweet’s Ballroom with all brand new instruments and I don’t know where they got the library from or if they played it by ear, but I went to see that band.
